question: Should older PowerShell installations adopt the proposed 30-second metadata and 600-second archive total deadlines, or must the legacy path preserve progressing downloads beyond ten minutes?
rationale: Older PowerShell cannot express the same per-read deadline, so bounding stalls necessarily introduces a total-duration compatibility policy that source inspection alone cannot select for maintainers.

options.title: Prove and retain the legacy budgets
options.body: Run representative Windows PowerShell 5.1 metadata and throttled-archive proof, then retain the 30/600-second fallback if normal slow transfers complete.

options.title: Accept the documented cap
options.body: Land the current fallback while explicitly accepting that legacy PowerShell downloads exceeding ten minutes can fail and use the existing installer error path.

options.title: Build a legacy stall-aware downloader
options.body: Replace TimeoutSec on older PowerShell with a larger custom transfer implementation that tracks progress, at the cost of substantially more installer complexity.

recommendation.title: Prove and retain the legacy budgets
recommendation.body: Run representative Windows PowerShell 5.1 metadata and throttled-archive proof, then retain the 30/600-second fallback if normal slow transfers complete.
